mcqs.question: What test tells you inheritance is the right tool for reusing another class's code?
options: Whether you can honestly say the subclass 'is a' kind of the base class, not just that it wants some of its code
Whether the subclass wants to reuse even one method from the other class
Whether the base class has fewer than five methods
Whether the two classes are defined in the same file
mcqs.explanation: Inheritance models an is-a relationship — a Car genuinely is a Vehicle — and that's what should justify it, not merely wanting to borrow some methods. Wanting code reuse alone, with no real is-a relationship, is the classic sign composition would be the safer choice instead.

mcqs.question: A subclass declares a `static` method with the same signature as one on its base class. Calling it through a base-class-typed reference to a subclass object, which version runs?
options: The subclass's version, resolved at runtime just like an overridden instance method
Both versions run, in base-to-subclass order
The base class's version, because static methods are hidden (shadowed), not overridden, and resolve by the reference's declared type at compile time
It throws a compile error, because static methods cannot share a signature across a hierarchy
mcqs.explanation: Static methods don't participate in runtime dispatch — there's no object instance (no `this`) to dispatch on — so a same-signature static method in a subclass merely hides the base version, resolved by the declared type at compile time. This is the opposite of how overridden instance methods behave, which is exactly the trap the slide names.

mcqs.question: Why do Java and C# forbid a class from extending more than one class, while still allowing it to implement multiple interfaces?
options: Because interfaces are faster to compile than classes
Because multiple interfaces were added to Java before multiple inheritance was considered
Because the JVM has a hard limit of one parent class per object in memory
Because multiple class inheritance creates real ambiguity in shared state and method resolution, while interfaces carry no state and side-step that problem
mcqs.explanation: Multiple class inheritance creates genuine ambiguity — which method wins when two parents define the same signature, and how many copies of shared ancestor state exist — that interfaces avoid entirely by carrying no fields and no ambiguous state to duplicate. This isn't a compilation-speed or memory-layout artifact; it's a deliberate design choice to avoid the diamond problem.

mcqs.question: When you call `new SportsCar()` in a hierarchy `Vehicle → Car → SportsCar`, in what order do the constructors run?
options: SportsCar, then Car, then Vehicle
Vehicle, then Car, then SportsCar
All three run simultaneously
Only SportsCar's constructor runs; the others are skipped unless explicitly called
mcqs.explanation: Base class constructors always run before the derived class constructor's own body, base-to-derived, so Vehicle initializes first, then Car, then SportsCar's own body — this guarantees base-class fields exist before subclass logic that might depend on them runs. Constructors aren't skipped implicitly; each level's constructor runs unless the language specifically allows omitting a no-arg base call.

mcqs.question: A base class's `refuel()` method is changed to call an overridable `checkTank()` twice instead of once, with no change to any public signature. A subclass that overrode `checkTank()` assuming one call now misbehaves. What does this illustrate?
options: The subclass has a bug unrelated to the base class change
Java's access modifiers are broken and need a bug report
The fragile base class problem — a base class's internal behavior, not just its signatures, is effectively part of its contract with subclasses
The subclass should never have used inheritance in the first place, regardless of any other design factor
mcqs.explanation: The subclass depended on behavior (call frequency of an overridable method) the base class author considered an internal detail, so a seemingly safe change silently broke it — this is exactly the fragile base class problem, not a subclass bug or a language defect. It's a real argument for composition, but it doesn't mean inheritance was categorically wrong to use here.
